Author_or_Organisation: Deori, C.; Begum, S. S.; Mao, A. A.
Title: Ethnobotany of Sujen—a local rice beer of Deori tribe of Assam
Publication_or_Source_Type: Research article; Indian Journal of Traditional Knowledge 6(1), 121–125
Geographic_Scope: Sunpura Deori gaon (Sadiya, Tinsukia); Kololuwah (Dibrugarh); Rajabari (Sivasagar)
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Sujen and Mod pitha starter
Claims_Supported: Primary ethnobotanical field study: 2003–2004 survey in Sunpura Deori gaon, Sadiya (Tinsukia); Kololuwah (Dibrugarh); Rajabari (Sivasagar). Interviewed regular Sujen makers and observed preparation. Reports 32 Mod pitha plant taxa, of which 20 were called essential and the remainder flavouring. Starter: 3–5 kg rice soaked about 2 h, mixed with sun-dried plant parts, ground/sieved; 2–3 old Mod pitha inoculate; cakes dried above fireplace for a couple of weeks and stored 2–3 months. Sujen: 4–5 kg rice cooked with rice husk, mixed with 2–3 powdered cakes, fermented in smoked earthen Koloh for 3–4 days in summer/about a week in winter, filtered through Sakoni. Fresh Sujen reportedly stores 2–3 weeks in summer and up to one month in winter. The paper itself says microbial/nutritional study is still needed.
Limitations_or_Caveats: No household count, respondent count or village-to-plant matrix. The 32 taxa are listed for the three-village study as a whole; not 32 species per village. Authors report historical use of over 100 plants but current survey collected 32, with 20 described as essential. Botanical identifications consult BSI Eastern Circle herbarium; individual voucher numbers are not published. Traditional beliefs about health and ritual are not clinical evidence. The paper warns that Citrus species are believed to spoil Sujen but says this needs scientific study. Do not treat fireplace-dried starter, storage durations or any process as a modern food-safety protocol.

Author_or_Organisation: Deka, D.; Sarma, G. C.
Title: Traditionally used herbs in the preparation of rice-beer by the Rabha tribe of Goalpara district, Assam
Publication_or_Source_Type: Research article; Indian Journal of Traditional Knowledge 9(3), 459–462
Geographic_Scope: Goalpara district, Assam
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Rabha rice beer and starter herbs
Claims_Supported: Primary ethnobotanical field survey of older experienced Rabha men and women in different villages of Goalpara district; exact village names, survey dates, informant count and herbarium voucher numbers are not reported. Ten plant taxa are listed for Rabha starter-cake preparation with community-language labels assigned to Rangdaniya, Maitori and Pati sub-tribes. Starter cake is called bakhor, surachi or phap; fermented drink choko or jonga-mod. Cooked rice + powdered starter is fermented in earthen jonga with bamboo-net janthi; 4–5 days summer, 7–8 winter. First drink is choko; re-fermentation with water and starter followed by pot-still distillation yields fotika. Boro rice preparation is described as sachotia mod; eating rice and beer together is juguli.
Limitations_or_Caveats: The study says 'different villages' in Goalpara but does not name them or give a sample/plant-to-village matrix, survey dates, sample size, or voucher numbers. The table lists ten starter-plant taxa; Heteropogon contortus is described as a drying-bed substrate, not one of the ten ingredient taxa. Musa balbisiana is used to seal the vessel; Ricinus communis leaf and charcoal are placed on the lid; Lagenaria siceraria is a collection scoop; Corchorus capsularis fibre and mud seal the distillation apparatus. Do not count these equipment/sealing uses as starter ingredients. The medicinal/curative statements are community beliefs and author reports, not clinical or safety evidence. Paper prints Cleodendrum viscosum and Ochthochloa coracana; preserve source spelling pending botanical verification.

Author_or_Organisation: Keot, Jyotshna; Bora, Sudipta Sankar; Kangabam, Rajiv Das; Barooah, Madhumita
Title: Assessment of microbial quality and health risks associated with traditional rice wine starter Xaj-pitha of Assam, India: a step towards defined and controlled fermentation
Publication_or_Source_Type: Research article; 3 Biotech 10, 64; DOI 10.1007/s13205-020-2059-z
Geographic_Scope: Twelve clusters across six Upper Brahmaputra Valley districts: Tinsukia, Dibrugarh, Sivasagar, Jorhat, Lakhimpur and Dhemaji; named clusters include Margherita, Sadiya, Moran, Naharkatiya, Bokota, Sonari, Titabar, Nimati, Bihpuria, Dhakuakhana, Bordoloni and Silapathar
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Ahom Xaj-pitha starter culture; experimental Xaj fermentation and defined mixed-culture development
Claims_Supported: Full text: 60 Xaj-pitha samples (5 per cluster, 2 clusters in each of 6 districts); 12 cluster composites for culture-based diversity, and one representative Titabar/Jorhat composite for WGS. Reports district/cluster microbial counts, seven-day fermentation dynamics, contaminants, 22 mould strains (13 amylase-positive; four selected), eight yeast isolates, strain-level safety/functionality screening and a candidate defined consortium of Amylomyces rouxii ABT82, Saccharomycopsis fibuligera ADJ4 and Saccharomyces cerevisiae ABT-Y1J. Full audit: research/assam/src024-keot-2020-xaj-pitha-fulltext-audit-2026-11-04.md.
Limitations_or_Caveats: Not a statewide or cross-community survey. One composite, not all 60 samples, underwent metagenomic sequencing. The Titabar WGS component reuses the same underlying dataset reported in SRC-023 (Bora et al. 2016): same MG-RAST identifier and distinctive sequence totals; count as one shared WGS dataset, not independent replication. The 60-sample culture-based survey and 12 cluster composites remain additional separate evidence. Exact sample-code crosswalk is not published. See research/assam/src023-src024-xaj-pitha-metagenome-dataset-reuse-audit-2026-11-04.md. Culture counts and organism detection are starter-specific; not proof of all taxa in finished beverage or universal consumer risk. Two yeast strains showed biogenic-amine production ability; all tested mould cultures were negative for aflatoxin only, not all mycotoxins. Candidate defined consortium is experimental, not shown to be household-adopted or a universal validated safe starter. No sample-to-household identities or full producer-level process records.

Author_or_Organisation: Das, R.; Medhi, M. C.; Tamang, B.
Title: Microbial diversity and its links to retinol pathways and aroma compounds in ethnic fermented rice beverages of Assam
Publication_or_Source_Type: Peer-reviewed research article, AMB Express 16, article 91
Geographic_Scope: Pukia, Dhemaji district (Black Rohi Modh BR and Rohi Modh RH); Kaljar, Baksa district (Jou Bidwi JOU); Jamuuri Panchali, Dhemaji district (Sai Mod SM); sample coordinates referenced in Supplementary File ST1
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Black Rohi Modh; Rohi Modh; Jou Bidwi; Sai Mod; household batch-level microbiome, physicochemical and metabolomic comparisons
Claims_Supported: Full text documents 12 sample units representing four beverages, but explicitly states each beverage was collected once as one authentic household batch; triplicates are technical, not independent biological replicates. BR and RH both sampled in Pukia, Dhemaji; JOU in Kaljar, Baksa; SM in Jamuuri Panchali, Dhemaji. The paper reports black-rice BR and common-rice RH separately, HPLC ethanol, DPPH/FRAP, microbial isolates, metagenomic profiles and GC-MS/MS metabolomics. Supplement ST1 contains sample codes and GPS coordinates; main-text map identifies Pukia for BR and RH. The article's Data Availability statement deposits raw shotgun-metagenomic data under NCBI BioProject PRJNA1284041; Sanger sequence accessions are provided with organism/yeast labels in Fig. 3. A structured summary of aggregate microbiome/metabolome metrics is stored in `research/assam/src046-microbiome-metabolome-summary.csv`.
Limitations_or_Caveats: The source labels the producer community broadly as Kachari; exact subcommunity and household identities are not established in the accessible main text. BR is one household batch and may be a black-rice variant of Rohi rather than a distinct locally named tradition. No sample-specific starter recipe or complete fermentation sequence for BR is provided; the article's general Rohi Modh account mentions Bora chaul and aaroi. Technical replicates do not provide biological replication; statistics and correlations are exploratory with n=4 independent product batches. HPLC and GC-MS/MS ethanol estimates differ and must remain separate. Antioxidant assays are in-vitro and not clinical health evidence. Retinol pathway annotations indicate predicted microbial metabolic potential, not direct vitamin A production. Supplementary GPS and detailed ST2-ST5 data require separate extraction; the DOCX link was not accessible in this pass. Supplementary File ST1 (sample GPS) and ST2–ST5 (proximate, isolate, metataxonomy and metabolomics data) are referenced by the publisher, but the DOCX was not retrieved in this pass. Raw shotgun metagenomic reads are separately cited by the article under BioProject PRJNA1284041; that accession has not yet been expanded into individual SRA run/sample records. 2026-11-07 recheck: full article text directly confirms the JOU sample locality Kaljar, Baksa and SM sample locality Jamuuri Panchali, Dhemaji; both are single-household batch samples. Place rows ASM-PL-117/118 preserve these source-reported collection sites without asserting village-wide or current production.

Publication_or_Source_Type: Original research article; Ethnobotany Research and Applications 34:1–31
Geographic_Scope: Jorhat district, Assam; ten named villages visited March 2024–2025: Charighoria, Upor Kareng, Kalbari, Neulgaon, Bormukoli, Bahfalla, Bor pomua gaon, Kumarbari gaon, Jeng rai Chapori and Kawoimari Bonoria Mishing Gaon. Claims_Supported: Full text reviewed (published 21 June 2026; DOI 10.32859/era.34.75.1-31): field survey in ten named Mising-dominant Jorhat villages (Charighoria, Upor Kareng, Kalbari, Neulgaon, Bormukoli, Bahfalla, Borpomua gaon, Kumarbari gaon, Jengrai Chapori, Kawoimari Bonoria Mishing Gaon), visited monthly for 12 consecutive months during March 2024–2025; 50 informants (17 men, 33 women). The paper does not map beverage forms to individual villages or informants. It states no voucher specimens were deposited.

Author_or_Organisation: Saikia, B.; Tag, H.; Das, A. K.

Publication_or_Source_Type: Primary research article; Indian Journal of Traditional Knowledge 6(1):126–132
Geographic_Scope: Tai-Ahom dominant rural areas of North Lakhimpur district, Assam; fieldwork 2005–2006; at least 15 local people interviewed; plants collected and deposited at Rajiv Gandhi University Botany Herbarium

Study also records 9 Ahu and 8 Sali rice varieties. Beverage processing fieldwork in North Lakhimpur during 2005–2006; at least 15 local people interviewed; plants identified using Indian Flora and deposited at Rajiv Gandhi University Botany Herbarium.
Limitations_or_Caveats: Paper reports the beverage as Sajpani (Tai) and Laopani (Assamese); it does not use Xajpani or Koloh pani in its beverage description. Historical source; no modern safety or chemical validation.

Community-reported medicinal uses are not clinical evidence, and conservation effects are not established causally by the qualitative design. Reports 16 yeast strains (9 Saccharomyces cerevisiae, 3 Saccharomycopsis fibuligera, 4 Candida tropicalis) and two filamentous fungi (Aspergillus oryzae, A. niger); sequence accessions MK110643, MK110642 and MK110644. Detailed extraction in research/assam/src-108-assam-mycoflora-sample-audit.md.
Limitations_or_Caveats: Abstract's seven-district list conflicts with six-district body; no sample-to-starter or sample-to-site matrix. Nine samples are not a statewide census. Organism detections do not establish presence in all samples or finished beverages. Discussion's C. tropicalis risk interpretation is not an epidemiological or finished-product exposure study. Preserve the unresolved geographic discrepancy and seek the original sample register/author clarification. ASM-GAP-053 remains Open.

Author_or_Organisation: Chakrabarty, Jayasree
Title: Identification of Yeast Strain Isolated from Nduiyi of Dima Hasao District of Assam, India
Publication_or_Source_Type: Research article; International Journal of Current Microbiology and Applied Sciences 6(3):587–594; DOI 10.20546/ijcmas.2017.603.068
Geographic_Scope: Dima Hasao district; Jeme Naga localities explicitly named: Lodi Basti, Asalu, Nutan Gunjung, Boro Haflong and Lisong/Laisong Basti; Table 1 sample collection sites: Haflong Bazaar and Lodi Basti for Nduiyi starter, Haflong Bazaar and Laisong Basti for Nduijao beverage
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Nduiyi mixed amylolytic starter; Nduijao sweet-sour alcoholic beverage
Claims_Supported: Full-text audit (2026-11-20): Nduiyi is described as a Jeme Naga starter for Nduijao. Starter recipe: sticky rice soaked 9–10 h, crushed with either Albizia myriophylla bark or Saccharum officinarum leaves and 2–3% previous Nduiyi as mother culture; water added to form paste; cakes kneaded, held 1–3 days at 25–30°C, sun-dried 2–3 days and stored dry for more than one year. Starter cakes described as 1.1–10.1 cm diameter and 15–25 g. Table 1: Nduiyi samples, Haflong Bazaar n=2 and Lodi Basti n=2; Nduijao samples, Haflong Bazaar n=2 and Laisong Basti n=2. Microbial populations reported as log CFU/g. Nduijao pH 4.3±0.1, titratable acidity 0.44±0.01 (unit not stated in prose) and alcohol 4–6% (reported study range). Starter isolates identified phenotypically as Saccharomyces cerevisiae (DHN:Y1/Y2) and Candida glabrata (DHN:Y3/Y4). Paper states rural women produce Nduiyi in Lodi, Asalu, Nutan Gunjung, Boro Haflong and Lisong Basti; market sale also reported. The paper's prose spelling Lisong differs from Table 1's Laisong.
Limitations_or_Caveats: Four starter samples are represented by two collection localities (Haflong Bazaar and Lodi Basti, n=2 each); Table 1 separately reports four finished Nduijao samples (Haflong Bazaar and Laisong Basti, n=2 each). Do not describe this as only four total samples across both products. The five named starter-production localities are a source-reported list, not a verified current prevalence census. Laisong/Lisong equivalence is unresolved. Haflong Bazaar is a market/sample collection site, not a village-level production estimate. Nduiyi starter ingredients are not a complete Nduijao beverage recipe. The paper's claims about tonic/post-natal benefits and safety are not clinical evidence. Alcohol and pH values are source-specific, not universal specifications or safety guidance. Keep Nduijao distinct from Zeme Nduizou/Zao/Zou pending community terminology evidence. Detailed audit: research/assam/src109-nduiyi-nduijao-chakrabarty-2017-fulltext-audit-2026-11-20.md.

Author_or_Organisation: Yumnam, H.; Hazarika, P.; Sharma, I.

Geographic_Scope: Southern Assam; five community cohorts; Zeme Naga cohort described in study as Cachar distribution

Author_or_Organisation: Atungbou, N.

Exact surrounding clauses and current legal status should be checked against the complete Gazette text.

Geographic_Scope: Bodoland Territorial Region, Assam (site-level heritage framing; not a verified legal production boundary)
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Three registered Bodo Jou beverages; Amao starter, traditional process descriptions, reported measurements and cultural contexts
Claims_Supported: Jou Gishi page describes cooked rice, Amao, banana-leaf cooling, vessel/sieve names, timing and reports pH ~4.21 and 5–6.4% alcohol; Jou Gwran page describes a reported fermentation/distillation sequence and repeats ~16.11% alcohol. The current migrated site (same Trust identity, Trust Deed 2025/IGR085/4/11) adds a product page for Maibra Jou Bidwi: half-cooked Maibra rice, Amao, 1–2 days initial stage, 5–7 days until dark juice forms, then a claimed 3-month-to-one-year-or-longer maturation before harvest. Site conflates certificate numbers 648–650 with application/GI numbers, while official registry application numbers are 968–970. Do not infer legal specifications, universal recipes, village production, or clinical health benefits. The migrated site repeats the certificate/application-number error on all three pages: GI/certificate numbers 648–650 are labelled as application numbers, whereas official IP India application IDs are 968–970. Its About page's holder claim (Bodo Traditional Brewer's Association) differs from the official application-detail pages' applicant field (Bodo Geographical Indication Board); registered-proprietor status remains unverified because the official Part A PDF is currently unavailable. The site's 'Verification Status: VERIFIED' is self-declared. The Maibra 3-month-to-one-year maturation, 1:1 kg starter ratio and health claims are not legal specifications or independently measured results.

Author_or_Organisation: Yumnam, Hanna; Hazarika, Parijat; Sharma, Indu
Title: Metagenomic insights into traditional fermentation of rice-based beverages among ethnic tribes in southern Assam, Northeast India
Publication_or_Source_Type: Original research article; Frontiers in Microbiology 15:1410098
Geographic_Scope: Southern Assam; five community cohorts; exact sample villages and sample-specific districts not reported in accessible main text
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Zeme Naga Zao/Zou; Dimasa Kachari Judima; Hmar Zu; Karbi Hor Alank; Tea-tribe Haria
Claims_Supported: Fifteen traditionally prepared, non-commercial pre-distillation beverage samples (three per community cohort) are stated in the article. The study used Illumina MiSeq bacterial 16S rRNA V3–V4 amplicon sequencing. NCBI BioProject PRJNA1017140 resolves to SRA Study SRP460503, five BioSamples and five experiments/runs (one per cohort: SRR26058871–SRR26058875); sample names TT, DMK, ZN, K1, HM. BioSample records give dates from 2022-06-21 to 2022-07-25, but only geographic location 'India' and the same repeated coordinate pair 20.59 N, 78.96 E for all five; they also link to PRJNA994679.
Limitations_or_Caveats: Despite title/terminology, method is targeted bacterial 16S V3–V4 amplicon sequencing, not untargeted shotgun metagenomics; no fungal ITS profiling. Major unresolved discrepancy: paper states 15 collected samples (3/cohort), while NCBI lists only 5 BioSamples and 5 SRA runs (one/cohort); pooling vs incomplete deposition is not established. BioSample geography is not locality-grade: all five repeat 20.59 N, 78.96 E and say only India; do not use as southern Assam sample coordinates. Each BioSample also links to PRJNA994679, relationship unverified. Exact villages, producer households and sample-to-village mapping not disclosed. Cohort tables aggregate results. No beverage-specific taxon abundance values transcribed from plotted figure. PICRUSt outputs are inferred functions, not measured genes/metabolites. Article contains inconsistent Zao/Zou spelling and statistical-text inconsistency: unweighted UniFrac sentence reports p>0.05 while calling it significant; PERMANOVA phylum-level p=0.2 is not significant. Do not make health/probiotic/safety claims. A second BioProject (PRJNA994679) is linked from each of the five BioSamples; its title/description refer to shotgun metagenomics of fermented rice products from southern Assam and its project page lists 10 experiments/6 BioSamples, but it also links an apparently unrelated yak gut virome publication. Relationship to SRC-132 and overlap with its samples remain unresolved; do not merge or treat as evidence that the 2024 article performed shotgun sequencing.

Author_or_Organisation: Basumatary, Z.; Saha, S.; Chaudhuri, S.; Ray, S.; Nayak, P. K.; Sen Maiti, S.

Author_or_Organisation: Pegu, Rajeswar; Gogoi, Jitu; Tamuli, Ajit K.; Teron, Robindra
Title: Apong, an Alcoholic Beverage of Cultural Significance of the Mising Community of Northeast India
Publication_or_Source_Type: Primary qualitative/cultural and process study; Global Journal of Interdisciplinary Social Sciences 2(6):12–17

Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Nogin Apong; Po:ro Apong / Saimod; E’pob starter; Ta:suk and Korai extraction
Claims_Supported: Full-text audit completed 2026-11-04. Reports participatory interviews, group discussions and observation; plant collection/identification and voucher preparation are described. Author_or_Organisation: Borkotoky, Babita Phukan; Neog, Mridula; Barua, Iswar Chandra
Title: Mishing’s Apong – An Intangible Cultural Heritage of Assam
Publication_or_Source_Type: Research article reproduced in The Exalted Edition / IJHEPS, Issue 7, digital pp. 59–63; ISSN 2320-2955
Geographic_Scope: Mising-dominated areas of Jorhat district, Assam; five named villages: Sirum, Budubari, Boloma, Bhomoraguri and Arunamukh
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Nogin Apong; Po:ro Apong / Saimod; Epop / Epoppitha starter culture
Claims_Supported: Full article text retrieved in digital issue. Repeated survey in Jorhat; prepared starter and beverages collected mostly from five named villages; plant collection April–June 2011 and 2012; voucher specimens reportedly deposited in Kakojan College Herbarium after identification with AAU Jorhat Weed Herbarium and BSI Eastern Circle, Shillong. Authors claim 51 plant species in 39 genera and 31 families, but the Table 1 plant inventory is not reliably exposed in the accessible text layer and no plant rows have been transcribed. Starter method: plant parts sun-dried 2–3 days, ground, mixed with soaked rice and old Epop, cakes 2–5 cm, incubated about 3 days on bamboo frame 1.5 m above kitchen fire and sun-dried 2–3 days; claimed storage about two months. Nogin: tightly cooked rice, 4–8 Epop/kg, 3–4 days in pots. Po:ro: specially burnt rice-husk/hay ash mixed with cooked rice before starter until rice blackens; pot fermentation 15–20 days; water percolation through banana-leaf-lined conical bamboo frame; filtrate collected in earthen pots. Microbiology: three Saccharomyces species and one each Mucor and Rhizopus reported from starter culture; authors report no Enterobacteriaceae or lactic-acid bacteria growth on their selected culture media. Reported viable yeast/mould count 118 × 10^7 per ml original culture sample. Article reports 5% alcohol in both Apong varieties; Nogin higher carbohydrate, protein, fat and calorific value than Po:ro; about 11 free amino acids reported in both.
Limitations_or_Caveats: Digital magazine/flipbook reproduction rather than a publisher-hosted journal archive; publication year is unresolved because the masthead says January 2014 while page 2 says January 2015, FlipHTML5 records publication on 17 January 2015, and the Kakojan College author profile lists it in 2015. Use 2014 as the printed issue year; retain the institutional 2015 profile discrepancy. The article’s Table 1 is not reliably available as text; do not invent or transcribe 51 plant names from secondary snippets. The authors describe extensive/repeated survey but give no informant or household count and no village-by-village allocation. Five villages are stated as the main collection sites; do not imply all 51 taxa occur at each village. Voucher deposition is stated but no accession numbers are supplied. Microbial identification is only to the group or lowest possible genera in methods; reported organism counts are not equivalent to modern molecular species identification. Negative culture results apply only to the media/incubation conditions used. Biochemical results are source-specific; no health benefit or food-safety inference is justified. The 5% alcohol value is not a universal specification and differs from other Po:ro studies.

Author_or_Organisation: Pawe, Dimbo; Gogoi, Rajib
Title: Ethnobotany of Poro Apong or Chai Mod — A local rice beer of Mishing tribes of Assam
Publication_or_Source_Type: Primary ethnobotanical article; NeBIO: An International Journal of Environment and Biodiversity 4(2):46–49; full text readable on ResearchGate
Geographic_Scope: Mishing-dominated localities in Lakhimpur and Sonitpur districts, Assam; seven selected villages named: Dhunaguri, Badati, Bongalmora, Chamaguri Temona, Luitmukh, Kathalkuchi and Rajbari
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Poro Apong / Chai Mod; comparative mention of Nogin Apong; Poro-specific Apob starter culture
Claims_Supported: Full text recovered. Authors report interviews with villagers who regularly prepare Poro and direct observation of the complete method; plant collections identified with confirmation at BSI Shillong herbarium (ASSAM) and Itanagar (ARUN). Table 1 accounts for all 28 botanical taxa: serials 1–24 (24 taxa), serial 25 contains two separately named Thelypteris taxa, and serials 27–28 (2 taxa); serial 26 is a numbering omission, not evidence of a missing taxon. Inventory: research/assam/src170-pawe-gogoi-2013-poro-apob-28-taxon-inventory.csv. Source-specific process: 2–4 kg rice soaked 2–3 h for Apob; cakes dried above kitchen fireplace 3–5 days; Poro mash includes straw/rice-husk ash and 4–5 crushed Apob cakes; fermentation 7–12 days by season (sometimes over a month), then water filtration/re-filtration through banana-leaf/straw-lined Tasuk until brown.
Limitations_or_Caveats: No field dates, informant count, voucher accession numbers/collector numbers or plant-by-village matrix. Full-text audit confirms the article's exact wording: selected villages Dhunaguri, Badati, Bongalmora, Chamaguri Temona, Luitmukh, Kathalkuchi and Rajbari; interviews with regular Poro Apong preparers; direct observation of the full method; final plant identification confirmation at BSI Shillong (ASSAM) and Itanagar (ARUN). It does not report a missing plant taxon: 28 taxa are present when both Thelypteris species printed under serial 25 are counted separately. Serial 26 is a numbering omission. Priority: request survey dates, informant/household counts, collector and accession numbers, vouchers, and author confirmation of the numbering omission; cross-check verbatim names separately against current taxonomic authorities. Full audit: research/assam/src170-pawe-gogoi-2013-poro-apob-acquisition-audit-2026-11-17.md. Table numbering skips 26; the two taxa in row 25 explain the reported 28 species if counted separately, but the article does not explain the numbering gap. Several printed taxon/family spellings are retained verbatim. The seven named villages are study sites only; no plant can be assigned to an individual village. The article's traditional medicinal claims are not clinical or safety evidence. The recovered method describes filtration through Tasuk, not distillation; do not generalize across households or reconcile conflicting accounts by inference. Full audit: research/assam/src170-pawe-gogoi-2013-poro-apong-acquisition-audit.md.

Title: Fermentation optimization for a probiotic local northeastern Indian rice beer and application to local cassava and plantain beer production
Publication_or_Source_Type: Research article; Journal of the Institute of Brewing 121(2):273–282; DOI 10.1002/jib.211
Geographic_Scope: Tezpur University laboratory fermentation study; no village-level beverage sample locality stated
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Laboratory rice-beer fermentation using Saccharomyces cerevisiae ATCC 9763, Aspergillus oryzae ATCC 10124 and Lactobacillus plantarum ATCC 8014; response-surface optimisation
Claims_Supported: The primary publisher full text describes a controlled laboratory study using rice (Oryza sativa var. Mahsuri), cassava and plantain substrates. Rice and cassava were procured from Assam Agricultural University (26°43'N, 94°11'E); plantains came from a Tezpur University experimental plot (26°42'N, 92°49'E). The researchers used laboratory microbial strains and a 13-run central composite rotatable design to optimise fermentation time and temperature; predicted optimum was 143 h at 33°C. This is process-engineering evidence, not a survey of household rice-beer production localities.
Limitations_or_Caveats: The coordinates refer to crop procurement/experimental facilities, not traditional rice-beer producer villages or beverage collection sites. The paper does not identify a community, traditional starter-cake sample, household, village of beverage production or Charaideo location. Do not map Assam Agricultural University coordinates as a rice-beer production locality. No Charaideo beverage-place row is justified.

Author_or_Organisation: Das, Arup Jyoti; Khawas, Prerna; Miyaji, Tatsuro; Deka, Sankar Chandra
Title: Phytochemical Constituents, Attenuated Total Reflectance Fourier Transform Infrared Analysis and Antimicrobial Activity of Four Plant Leaves Used for Preparing Rice Beer in Assam, India
Publication_or_Source_Type: Research article; International Journal of Food Properties 19(9):2087–2101; DOI 10.1080/10942912.2015.1104695
Geographic_Scope: Plant material collected from Tezpur University botanical gardens, Assam; no traditional producer-village locality
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Leaves of Artocarpus heterophyllus, Cyclosorus extensa, Oldenlandia corymbosa and Alpinia malaccensis; phytochemical and in-vitro antimicrobial assays
Claims_Supported: The publisher full text states that the four plant species were collected from the botanical gardens of Tezpur University campus and taxonomically identified by the Department of Botany, Darrang College, Tezpur. It evaluates phytochemical composition and antimicrobial activity of extracts. It clarifies that leaves are used in preparing starter cakes, not directly added to the fermentation mixture.
Limitations_or_Caveats: This is a plant-extract laboratory study, not a village-level ethnobotanical survey. The collection location is the university botanical garden, not the traditional harvesting locality of the plants or a rice-beer producer village. It cannot be used to assign starter-plant occurrence to Charaideo or any specific community locality. Do not confuse the botanical garden collection with the natural source of traditional ingredients. The publisher article's reference list explicitly cites a “Final Report of the R&D project ‘Quality Improvement of Traditional Method of Rice Beer Production by the Tribal People of North-East India’”, submitted to MoFPI by Tezpur University. This confirms that a final report for the 12/MFPI/R&D/2009 project existed and was cited by 2016, but the citation supplies no report URL, date, pagination or field-site annex. The referenced report must not be conflated with the separate nine-page 97/MFPI/R&D/2012 report (SRC-258). No beverage-place row is justified.

Author_or_Organisation: Konwar, Surajeet; Doimari, Rituparna; Gogoi, Monisha; Gogoi, Pranati
Title: Ethnomedicinal plants use by the Ahom and Bodo community in human health management in Charaideo district of Upper Assam, North East India
Publication_or_Source_Type: Research article; Journal of Bioresources 12(2):72–77; DOI 10.5281/zenodo.14892099

Claims_Supported: The article reports participant observation, interviews and focus-group discussions with 58 Ahom and Bodo informants across fifteen named Charaideo villages between January 2023 and May 2024. Author_or_Organisation: Mili, Rajiv; Sundriyal, R. C.
Title: ÉPOP (traditional starter culture): a complex composition of plant resources prepared by the Misings of Assam, Northeast India
Publication_or_Source_Type: Research article; Journal of Ethnic Foods 10:47; DOI 10.1186/s42779-023-00214-2
Geographic_Scope: Formal survey: 15 randomly selected villages in Sivasagar district; intensive study villages Majorbari and Ligiribari. Acknowledgements additionally thank villagers of Gumutha, Ramnagar and Balikuthi of Charaideo for support during field visits; their role/site-specific research contribution is not described.
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Mising Apong starter culture (ÉPOP); 31 plant species and detailed preparation/collection practices; potential Charaideo fieldwork acknowledgement requiring author clarification
Claims_Supported: The article explicitly states that it investigated Mising ÉPOP preparation for Apong and records 31 starter-culture plant species. Methods say the extensive survey covered 15 randomly selected villages in Sivasagar district and the two representative in-depth sites were Majorbari and Ligiribari. The acknowledgements separately thank villagers of Gumutha, Ramnagar and Balikuthi of Charaideo for support during field visits. The article's background/discussion further states at community-wide level that both Poro Apong and Nogin/Nogin Apong are occasionally used in rituals and rites for worshipped deities, and that Apong is used at spiritual, religious and social events. This is general Mising context, not a finding allocated to Charaideo or Ramnagar. The acknowledgement naming villagers of Gumutha, Ramnagar and Balikuthi remains a material lead that the research team had some field engagement/support in Charaideo, and the three village names should be retained verbatim for author clarification.
Limitations_or_Caveats: The article does not state that Gumutha, Ramnagar or Balikuthi were among the 15 survey villages, that Apong/ÉPOP or its ritual use was observed there, or that the 31-plant inventory derives from those Charaideo villages. The formal methods and map describe Sivasagar district and Majorbari/Ligiribari; acknowledgements alone cannot establish beverage production, starter-culture use, informants, or sample provenance in Charaideo. Do not create beverage/place rows or assign any of the 31 species to Charaideo. Ask the corresponding author to clarify the nature, dates and outputs of Charaideo field visits and whether beverage/starter-culture data were collected there.

Claims_Supported: The study documents Mising magico-religious plant knowledge associated with Dobur Uie and reports 30 plant species across 23 families. It explicitly describes Apong as a rice beer offered to spirits, sprinkled on the altar and ritual participants, and collected from households with rice, wild vegetables, chicken and pork as Ajenge dues. Fieldwork covered eight districts, including Sibsagar, during surveys based on 2009–2010 mopping-up work; researchers interviewed Mibus, healers, village heads and elders and collected herbarium vouchers at Dhemaji College. Separate from the 30-plant Dobur Uie inventory, the article explicitly identifies plant parts used in Apong preparation (including Ageratum conyzoides flowers, Ananas comosus tender leaf base, Artocarpus heterophyllus mature leaves, Asparagus racemosus tuberous roots in Dhemaji, Centella asiatica whole plant, Cinnamomum tamala leaves, Gomphostemma parviflora tender leaves, Kaempferia rotunda tubers, Leucas plukenetii leaves, Microsorum punctatum leaves in Dhemaji and Lakhimpur, Naravelia zeylanica leaves in Dhemaji, Oldenlandia corymbosa, Oryza sativa, Psidium guajava tender leaves, Pueraria tuberosa tuberous roots, and Scoparia dulcis leaves). Limitations_or_Caveats: The paper does not publish a village-by-village sampling frame, and its eight-district list does not identify Ramnagar or assign specific observations to present-day Charaideo. The 30-plant Dobur Uie inventory must remain distinct from the Apong-preparation plant list. Acorus calamus is described for ritual-site use, not as an Apong ingredient; the Dhemaji tuber entry is Asparagus racemosus. Do not create a Ramnagar place row or attribute any of the 30 plants to Ramnagar.

Author_or_Organisation: Boro, Nitesh; Narzary, Diganta
Title: Amylolytic Fungi in the Ethnic Beer Starter “emao” and Their Beer-Producing Attributes
Publication_or_Source_Type: Peer-reviewed original research; Frontiers in Sustainable Food Systems 6:869430; DOI 10.3389/fsufs.2022.869430
Geographic_Scope: One Emao starter sample collected from a local brewer at Rajapanichanda, Rani, Kamrup, Assam; traditional Jou control also collected from a local practitioner (control collection locality not specified)
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Bodo Emao starter; Jou control beverage; culturable fungal isolates and laboratory rice fermentations
Claims_Supported: One dried Emao sample was cultured; 50 fungal isolates were recovered, grouped morphologically into 11 groups, and one representative isolate per group sequenced (11 representatives). Ten species names assigned across the 11 isolates: Candida glabrata, Cyberlindnera fabianii, Hyphopichia burtonii, Mucor circinelloides, Mucor indicus, Penicillium citrinum, Rhodosporidiobolus ruineniae (two isolates), Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Saccharomycopsis fibuligera and Wickerhamomyces anomalus. Among the 50 recovered isolates, W. anomalus 24%, C. glabrata 16%, H. burtonii 16%; this is culturable isolate recovery composition, not direct starter community abundance. Five representative strains were amylase-positive and produced ethanol from soluble starch: Hbur_RF19, Sfib_RF11, Mind_RF25, Mcir_RF48, Pcit_RF32. Pure-culture rice fermentations (180 g dehusked glutinous rice; 2 g fresh fungal biomass in 30 mL water; triplicate; 30±1°C) yielded 3.17–7.30% v/v ethanol; four strains after 30 days, Mind_RF25 after 180 days. Traditional Jou control had 9.09±0.03% v/v ethanol and pH 3.78±0.01. ITS accessions OK073666–OK073676. Limitations_or_Caveats: This is a single starter sample, not a representative multi-village survey. The 50-isolate percentages are among culturable isolates recovered under this protocol, not relative abundance in the whole starter or beverage. Eleven representative isolates represent 11 morphology groups, not the full microbial community. Pure fungal isolate fermentations are controlled laboratory trials and do not reproduce the mixed traditional Emao fermentation. The traditional Jou control's collection locality and batch provenance are not specified. The 2021 study (SRC-309) names Panichanda, Rani, Kamrup, while this 2022 paper says Rajapanichanda, Rani, Kamrup; do not assume these are identical place strings without confirmation. Antibacterial inhibition in agar plates does not establish beverage safety, pathogen elimination or clinical benefit. Some reported isolate species, notably Candida glabrata and Penicillium citrinum, require strain-level safety evaluation before any food application. Detailed audit: research/assam/src310-boro-narzary-2022-emao-amylolytic-fungi-audit-2026-11-20.md.

Author_or_Organisation: Boro, Nitesh; Borah, Ashis; Sarma, Rajib L.; Narzary, Diganta
Title: Beer production potentiality of some non-Saccharomyces yeast obtained from a traditional beer starter emao
Publication_or_Source_Type: Peer-reviewed original research; Brazilian Journal of Microbiology 53(3):1515–1531; DOI 10.1007/s42770-022-00765-7; PMID 35488168; PMCID PMC9433491
Geographic_Scope: One one-month-old Emao starter sample collected from a Boro village named Boragari, Dotoma, Assam; district not stated in this paper
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Boro/Bodo Emao starter; isolated yeast/mould strains; laboratory rice-beer fermentations compared with Emao control
Claims_Supported: Fifty fungal colonies picked; ten representative morphotypes selected for identification and simultaneous saccharification and beer fermentation (SSBF) testing. Identified isolates: Hyphopichia burtonii (four isolates Hbur-FI38/FI44/FI47/FI68), Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Scer-FI51), Wickerhamomyces anomalus (Wano-FI52), Candida carpophila (Ccar-FI53), Mucor circinelloides (Mcir-FI60), Saccharomycopsis malanga (Smal-FI77/FI84). Author_or_Organisation: Gogoi, Girish
Title: Traditional knowledge on preparation of starter culture cakes and rice-beers by Chaodang community of upper Assam, India
Publication_or_Source_Type: Peer-reviewed research article; Emergent Life Sciences Research 7(1):63–75; DOI 10.31783/elsr.2021.716375
Geographic_Scope: Ten villages in Baghchung Development Block, Jorhat district, Assam; survey Jan–Jun 2020; GPS recorded and sampling map published
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Chaodang community; Saj/Laopani rice beer; Su-pitha/Modor-pitha starter cakes; Rohi mod first extraction; Choka mod second extraction
Claims_Supported: 80 traditional knowledge holders/key informants across ten randomly selected villages (eight key persons per village) interviewed with prior informed consent. Villages: Habungia Gaon, Jamuguri Gaon, Kumar Chaodang Gaon, Borbheta Gaon, Kebang Gaon, Baghmoria Gaon, Timtimia Gaon, Lojonia Gaon, Ujani Nonoi Gaon and Khoriachuk Gaon. Paper documents 81 plant species in 47 families used in Su-pitha; 50 species reported common across all ten villages, remaining 31 not common to all, and one village reported 61 species. Plant part data: leaves (46 species), whole plants (19), fronds (6), leaves+barks (2), young shoots (2), and several other part categories each for one species. Rice types: Bora (sticky), Chakuwa and normal Sali rice, sometimes mixed. Su-pitha method: plants gathered from homestead/tea gardens/private forests/roadsides/riversides/fields/natural forests; largest-quantity plant Amblovenatum opulentum sundried; normal Sali rice soaked 3–4 h, drained 1 h, mixed with washed plants, pounded in Dheki, sieved through bamboo and finer metal sieves, made into paste and ~2.5 cm cakes; old starter powder dusted on cakes; covered with paddy straw 4 days summer/6 days winter; air-dried 2–3 h then smoked over kitchen fire on Dhua chang/bamboo sieve for 2–3 days; stored usually 2–3 months. Saj process: cooked rice cooled on banana leaves; 3–5 Su-pitha cakes/kg rice; covered with banana leaves; 1–2 days summer or 3–4 winter; transferred to smoked/dried earthen pot for 5–7 days; add 1.5 L water/kg rice, wait 12 h, first extraction Rohi mod; add 1 L water to remaining fermented mass per kg, sieve second extraction Choka mod. The article states Choka mod is white, more turbid and lower in alcohol. Rice type affects reported colour/taste/strength. The article reports community plant taxonomy and use; Table 1 lists 81 taxa including *Amblovenatum opulentum*, *Lygodium* spp., *Centella asiatica*, *Hydrocotyle sibthorpioides*, *Mussaenda frondosa*, *Cannabis sativa* and *Croton tiglium*.
Limitations_or_Caveats: The article documents a survey and traditional knowledge, not controlled fermentation trials; no alcohol concentration values are measured for Saj, Rohi mod or Choka mod. 80 informants are eight key persons in each of ten villages; individual household/sample allocation and village-specific recipe matrices are not supplied. The article reports 81 plants in the publisher PDF/table and says 50 were common across all villages, but a secondary Academia metadata/text extraction reports 51 in its abstract; publisher PDF and Table 1 are used as controlling evidence, and the discrepancy is noted. No plant voucher accession numbers or herbarium deposit crosswalk are reported; plant identifications are described as based on floras. The article's “medicinal” and health claims are ethnographic statements, not clinical evidence or toxicological validation. Some listed taxa require specialist safety assessment; do not infer that every species is used in every batch, that plant quantity is standardized, or that every plant is safe to ingest. “Laopani” is a source-used label for this Chaodang Saj account and should not be merged with other Assam communities' Laopani/Sajpani records without terminology evidence. Current practice and present-day prices are not established by the 2020 fieldwork. Detailed audit: research/assam/src312-gogoi-2021-chaodang-saj-laopani-su-pitha-audit-2026-11-20.md.

Limitations_or_Caveats: Abstract lists seven districts, whereas the introduction says six; the exact district count is internally inconsistent. No nine-sample register, sample-to-district/village allocation, community attribution, sample IDs or starter-type-by-isolate matrix is supplied in accessible article text. Methods refer to dry starter cultures Xaaj pitha, Apong and Suzen (mod pitha); do not assign them to Ahom, Mishing, Tiwa or other communities without primary evidence. Sixteen yeast isolates are culture-dependent; only one representative from each yeast group appears to have been sequenced, so molecular confirmation is not isolate-by-isolate. A. niger identification is morphological in the article; only A. oryzae is stated as NCFT-confirmed. The article's statement about Candida tropicalis as a potential health hazard is a literature-based concern, not evidence of contamination level, pathogenicity in the sampled drinks, or a measured consumer risk. No finished-beverage alcohol, chemistry, toxin or safety testing reported. Detailed audit: research/assam/src313-saikia-2024-assam-mycroflora-nine-starter-survey-audit-2026-11-20.md.

Author_or_Organisation: Borah, Dipankar; Gogoi, Tridip; Sarma, Jintu; Borah, Punam Jyoti; Gohain, Bichitra; Mili, Chiran jib; Upadhyaya, Ankur; Basumatary, Jenima; Neog, Kasturi; Wangpan, Tonlong; Tangjang, Sumpam
Title: Compendium of plants used for preparation of traditional alcoholic beverages by four major ethnic communities of Assam, northeast India
Publication_or_Source_Type: Peer-reviewed ethnobotanical field research; Biodiversitas 22(4):2019–2031; DOI 10.13057/biodiv/d220451
Geographic_Scope: 32 villages across six districts: Baksa, Biswanath, Golaghat, Lakhimpur, Sivasagar and Sonitpur; fieldwork October 2019–March 2020; 202 respondents; no village list or sample-to-village allocation in article text
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Ahom: Haaj/Laupani, Haajpitha/Vekurpitha; Bodo: Jou/Bishi, Amao/Angkur; Karbi: Hor/Hor-alank, Thap; Mishing: Poro apong/Sai mod, Apoppitha
Claims_Supported: Plants collected in respondents' presence; identified using floras and regional herbarium comparisons; specimens submitted to Herbarium of Rajiv Gandhi University. Reports 129 plant species, 107 genera, 54 families; 39 species had prior reports and 90 were newly recorded for the four-community survey. Lamiaceae and Lauraceae eight species each; Asteraceae seven; Rubiaceae and Polygonaceae six each. Leaves comprise 88% of reported plant parts, twigs 4%, roots 3%. Starter cakes: plant materials washed fresh or dried; rice soaked 2–6 h and powdered; dried plant parts powdered and mixed with rice flour; small amount of old starter powder inoculates dough; small round balls dried and stored above fireplace. Thelypteris parasitica, Musa balbisiana and paddy hay are reported as coverings/storage protection. Generic rice beer method: cooked rice cooled on banana leaves in winnowing basket, powdered starter mixed, filled in vessel and sealed with banana/Alpinia leaves, straw and cloth; fermentation 5–9 days depending on season/climate; filtered. Po:ro apong special process: partially burn paddy husk and dry straw to ash; mix ash and powdered Apoppitha with boiled rice; ferment in smoked/blackened earthen pot sealed with straw and Thelypteris parasitica leaves for one to two weeks; extract through Ta:suk cone-shaped bamboo basket lined with banana leaves and paddy straw (Amrong), pouring cold then warm/hot water; filtrate collected as Apong. Distillation reported among Bodo, Karbi and Mishing, not Ahom; apparatus described with lower boiler, perforated earthen middle chamber/receiver and upper cold-water condenser.
Limitations_or_Caveats: 32 villages are not individually named in article text and there is no village-to-community/sample allocation. Respondents total 202 across all communities; community-specific counts are not provided. Supplementary Table S1 contains plant names, vernacular names, parts, voucher codes and prior literature, but those data are not a complete village-by-village recipe matrix. The main article says specimens submitted to Rajiv Gandhi University herbarium; do not claim all voucher codes are deposited there without checking supplement/curatorial register. 129 species are reported for four communities, not for each community separately. 90 “new” plants means newly recorded in this study's community-use dataset, not newly discovered botanical species. The paper's Table 2 uses broad labels (Ahom Haaj/Laupani; Bodo Jou/Bishi; Karbi Hor/Hor-alank; Mishing Poro apong/Sai mod) that should not collapse distinct canonical products or starter names in the archive. Po:ro apong is a special extraction/ash process and is not equivalent to generic fermented rice beer; filtration through Ta:suk is not distillation. Article includes ethnomedicinal rationale but no clinical efficacy, toxicology or finished-beverage safety validation. No alcohol concentrations or microbial measurements are reported. Detailed audit: research/assam/src314-borah-2021-four-community-129-plant-compendium-audit-2026-11-20.md.

Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Bodo, Karbi, Ahom, Deori, Rabha, Mising, Sonowal Kachari
Claims_Supported: Source-specific starter names and beverage preparation accounts; plant tables list botanical names, vernacular names, plant parts and ethnomedicinal-use claims. Limitations_or_Caveats: Although labelled a review article, the text reports specific field localities and acknowledges local informants; however, no transparent methods section, field dates, respondent numbers, village list, voucher catalogue or sample-to-plant crosswalk is supplied. It cites earlier sources including Saikia et al. 2007 (Tai Ahom), Deka & Sarma 2010 (Rabha), and Deori et al. 2007 (Sujen), so its overlap with those papers is not independent corroboration. The source's plant tables contain taxonomic, family, plant-part and ethnomedicinal transcription errors/inconsistencies; preserve printed values and do not treat ethnomedicinal claims as clinical evidence. Generic Mising Apong is not assigned to Noggin or Poro variants. Karbi Horlang should not automatically be equated with Hor-arak. No current prevalence, beverage chemistry, microbial testing or safety validation.

Author_or_Organisation: Baidya, Shilpa; Thakur, Bijay; Malunguja, Gisandu; Devi, Ashalata
Title: Changes of land use land cover and floristic composition in sacred forests of West Karbi Anglong district, Assam, India
Publication_or_Source_Type: Peer-reviewed floristic and land-cover study; Tropical Plant Research 7(2):296–308; DOI 10.22271/tpr.2020.v7.i2.035
Geographic_Scope: Bichikri and Harlong sacred forests, West Karbi Anglong district, Assam, India
Communities_or_Beverages_Covered: Regional sacred-forest flora; Bichikri tree inventory includes Ardisia arborea Koord. & Valeton; Bichikri herb inventory includes Phyllanthus amarus
Claims_Supported: Provides an independent published Assam report of the name Ardisia arborea at Bichikri sacred forest (frequency 2%, abundance 1, density 2 ha-1, basal area 0.09 m2 ha-1, IVI 3.33) and a separate record of Phyllanthus amarus in the Bichikri herb layer. Floristic sampling was 2017–2018. The study surveyed 116 plant species across both forests and provides site-specific inventory tables.
Limitations_or_Caveats: Not a study of Chaodang Saj or Su-pitha and does not corroborate SRC-312 household use. Methods state species names were recorded with caretaker knowledge and difficult specimens identified using Flora of Assam (Kanjilal & Bor 1938); nomenclature followed The Plant List. The accessible paper does not provide a voucher accession or diagnostic image for the Ardisia arborea record. Kew POWO and WFO list A. arborea native range as Jawa only, so the Assam report creates a literature-level conflict, not a resolved range extension or specimen authentication. Phyllanthus amarus at Bichikri does not identify the SRC-312 entry printed as P. niruri. Do not transfer either regional occurrence to the Chaodang field specimens.

Kew POWO and the MNHN type specimen place C. sympodialis in eastern Brazil; the Assam publication may reflect a repeated regional name/identification rather than a verified Assam occurrence of the Brazilian species. Do not infer that both communities use the same biological species or merge their knowledge records. Medicinal-use claims are source-reported only, not clinical evidence.
